title: Perf run 20261014-0357
heading: On a slow GPU, a move now appears in under half a second instead of over two
meta:
This run changed how the game’s board and the lobby send pictures to the GPU. On the bench’s software renderer, a move now appears about five times sooner, and joining a game shows the board in 1.6 s instead of 5.5 s. One headline measurement got 17% worse because of how it is timed, and that needs your decision. The changes are in PR #133; CI passes.

Run 2026-10-14, 03:57–07:15 UTC. Main at b1709f5, branch improve/20261014-0357. Measured in headless Chromium with SwiftShader (WebGL drawn on the CPU) on 4 CPUs. Every comparison is an A/B: the bench runs main and the branch back to back several times, and each back-to-back run is a pair. A change is called only when every pair moves the same way, by more than 5% and by more than the pairs disagree with each other.

items.title: Decide whether to keep the pacer, which makes one headline measurement 17% worse
items.body:
The run’s rule is that nothing may get slower than main beyond measured noise, and never by more than 3%. The headline measurement “A move landing, the player’s” is 17% slower on the branch, in every pair (1.16, 1.09, 1.31, 1.14). Two copies of identical code measured against each other gave +0.6% for the same measurement, so this is not noise. I kept the change anyway, and you can overrule that.

The change, called the pacer below, makes the game’s and the lobby’s canvases send a new picture to the GPU only after the GPU has finished the previous one. Before, a slow GPU received a new picture every display frame and fell further and further behind. The headline measurement stops the clock when a picture is handed to the GPU, not when the GPU has drawn it. With the pacer, the hand-over waits for the previous picture, so it happens later. The picture itself is finished about five times sooner:

items.recommend: Keep the pacer. Then change bench/primary.mjs so that the three move and selection headline measurements use the “drawn by the GPU” times, which CLAUDE.md allows for a moment measured differently. Those three rows can then no longer be compared with older runs.

items.title: Check how the lobby and the game’s entrance look on your phone
items.body:
With the pacer, the lobby’s motion keeps its real timing and a slow GPU draws fewer pictures of it. Before, a slow GPU also slowed the motion down. That is why the way into a game against the computer now takes 8.8 s instead of 15.4 s. On a GPU that keeps up, nothing changes: it draws every picture as before.

The bench can measure the timing but not the look. Recordings made with the showcase script are also no guide, because they step time frame by frame and the pacer then draws every frame. In those recordings the branch matches main frame for frame.

items.title: Two other measurements looked slower; neither is the branch’s
items.body:
“Start page answers its first click” was 22% slower in the final A/B (pairs 1.80, 1.29, 1.04, 0.92). The branch changes nothing on that path. When identical code was measured against itself at the start of the run, the same measurement came out 31% slower, so it varies this much on its own.

“The computer’s search speed” was 29% slower in the final A/B, on code the branch does not touch. I ran it again with 6 pairs: 5.5% slower, with the pairs going both ways (0.89, 1.00, 1.08, 0.92, 1.46, 1.06), so the bench does not call it. That is noise.

scoreboard.intro:
The bench’s headline measurements are the eleven moments a player waits for, listed in bench/primary.mjs. Against main, the branch is 1.173 times as fast over all eleven. Two are called better: joining a game (71% faster) and the computer’s first board frame (60% faster). None is called worse. Memory did not grow beyond the 5% limit: a reopened long game uses 1.0% more JavaScript heap.

The final A/B ran with uncommitted changes in the branch’s folder. They were the run’s own notes in bench/loop/, committed a minute later as cf92a12. No app or bench code was uncommitted.

items.title: The branch against the first recorded run: the 1.2× target is met
items.body: The run’s target was 1.2 times the speed of the first recorded run (92ce041). The branch reaches 1.344 times, over the nine headline measurements that the old code can also make (it had no computer player). The last run reached 0.893 times. One measurement is called worse than the first run: the desktop start page is 20% slower. Its first paint is 20% slower and it downloads 11% more, because the start page has grown since then (the computer player, the tutorial, the preview). A reopened long game uses 35% more heap than in the first run, which earlier runs already found.

items.title: How much the bench varies on identical code
items.body: The run began by measuring main against itself. That called the opponent’s move 49% faster on one side, with identical code. The frame that shows the move waited 14–290 ms behind frames the GPU already had queued, and the queue happened to differ between the sides. That queue is what the pacer removes.

items.title: The game’s and the lobby’s canvases wait for the GPU before sending the next picture
items.body:
Each canvas now places a marker (a WebGL fence) after each picture. A new picture is sent only when the GPU has passed the marker. Until then the canvas skips that frame and asks for the next one, while the motion keeps its real timing. The change is 70 lines in client/src/three/framePacer.tsx (commit a7cf4a4).

Review found two faults in it, fixed in f8ab886. After the WebGL context was lost and restored, the canvas could stop drawing for good; it now forgets its old marker. The warm-up of the game’s shaders could count a skipped frame as drawn; it now waits for a frame that was really drawn. A marker also holds a frame for at most 60 display frames, about one second. Each fix has a test that fails without it.

items.title: The bench times what the player sees
items.body:
• Each frame now records when the GPU finished drawing it, and the move and selection sections report that time beside the hand-over time.
  • The bench’s camera turn used to depend on how often frames came, so a faster page turned further. It now turns an exact angle.
  • The A/B rule ignored a pair whose value was 0, so it could call a change that one pair contradicted. The rule now has its own file and a test.
  • bench/run.mjs used to run something else when a flag was mistyped, overwrite the results and report success. It now stops with an error.
  • The computer section used to record empty results when the computer’s worker failed. It now stops with an error.

items.title: Silent failures now leave a message
items.body: The computer now logs an error when its search finds no move but the rules allow one. A saved computer game that cannot be read now logs why, because it is the only copy. The shader warm-up reports how it ended, and the bench shows that beside the first piece picked up.

items.title: Tests and checks that could pass on broken code now fail
items.body:
The e2e tests for games against the computer passed even with the computer’s search broken, because every fallback keeps the game going. They now fail on any fallback message, any page error, and any message sent to the server, which a computer game never uses. A deliberately broken search makes them fail. The test for a page whose 3D code fails to load now waits until the failure has happened before it checks the page.

Lint now catches timers called through globalThis or self, requestIdleCallback, new Date(), any use of __r3fState outside the game canvas, and click handlers in three/scene. Six deliberate violations all fail. CI now runs uv sync --locked, so a Python lock file that no longer matches pyproject.toml fails the build.

items.title: Phone, screen reader and security headers
items.body: On a phone held upright, the open move list covers the lower levels of the board. A tap elsewhere or the Escape key now closes it, as the game menu already does. A screen reader now reads each tutorial step aloud while the focus stays on the Next button. A new public/_headers file stops other websites from showing the game in a frame, stops browsers from guessing file types, and sends only the site’s name to links the player follows.

removed.intro: Nothing was deleted. Outside the run’s notes, the branch adds 815 lines and removes 103 in 40 files. Of these, the app gains 148 lines (70 of them the pacer), tests gain 388, the bench gains 161 and loses 52, and the lint configuration gains 60 and loses 29. The code grew for one speed change that players see, and for fixes, messages and checks.

items.title: Pacing the start page’s preview and the tutorial too
items.body: Five pairs on the start page showed no change: 1.002 times as fast overall, with no measurement called. The tutorial has no measurement. I reverted it. The patch is in bench/loop/patches/pace-preview-and-tutorial-FP2.patch.

choices.intro:
• I kept the pacer although one headline measurement got 17% worse, and left bench/primary.mjs unchanged for you to decide.
  • A frame waits for the GPU for at most 60 display frames, about one second.
  • When time is stepped frame by frame (the showcase recordings and the orbit e2e test), the pacer draws every frame.
  • The bench’s camera turn now turns an exact angle, so its “after a turn” measurements cannot be compared with earlier runs.
  • I added the security headers and uv sync --locked.
  • On a phone, the open move list closes on a tap elsewhere or Escape.
  • The computer’s fallbacks log as errors, and an unreadable saved game logs as a warning.
  • I did not research new libraries or dependency updates this run, because none of the project’s dependencies changed since the last run did.

notConfirmed.intro:
• The security headers on Cloudflare Pages. The sandbox cannot reach pages.dev, so I could not fetch them.
  • The pacer on a real phone GPU and in Safari. The bench renders in software only.
  • Whether the lobby’s fades, which run in the page rather than on the GPU, get ahead of the paced picture on a slow phone.
  • The full e2e suite on the final commit on this machine. It passed in CI, and it passed here on the pacer’s first commit except for one test that failed only because a font could not be loaded from the folder I used.
  • The start page’s first click with more pairs.

merge.intro: No other sessions worked on the repo, and main did not change during the run. ARCHITECTURE.md now describes the pacer and the security headers; CLAUDE.md is unchanged. I suggest one line in CLAUDE.md’s “Performance” section: the move and selection measurements time the hand-over to the GPU, and the “drawn by the GPU” measurements time the picture.

next.intro:

  2. Check every place that assumes a frame callback means a frame was drawn, now that frames can be skipped.
  3. Look again at the shader warm-up. In every final run the player’s first pick came before the warm-up started, so the first pick’s 92 ms is its own frame.
  4. Share the garden’s geometry data between the lobby and the game, after measuring how much of the join it costs.
  5. Give each page its own preload list, so game pages stop preloading the tutorial.
  6. The smaller items in the ledger: RV7, RV8, RV10, RV11, T20, M1′, D3 and SP.
